Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
The Apache Kafka clients are often wrapped by frameworks such as Spring. Kafka does this itself in Kafka Streams and Kafka Connect. There is no architected way of identifying clients running within such frameworks which can hinder problem determination.
When diagnosing an issue from the client logs, the application code is not directly calling the Kafka client. This means there's a mismatch between what the application developer wrote and how the Kafka client is being used. Behaviors such as retries or transactions can be implemented in the framework rather than the application. Having the information about whether a framework is being used can illuminate why the application is appearing to behave in a particular way.
Proposed Changes
Three client configurations are added which can be set by frameworks embedding Kafka clients (producer, consumer and admin). The configurations areclient framework name(the name of the framework),client framework version(the version of the framework) andclient framework ID(additional framework-specific context which may not be relevant to all frameworks). These are flowed to the broker in theApiVersionsrequest alongside the client software name and version providing more comprehensive context information about clients wrapped by frameworks.
The values are set using theCommonClientConfigs.CLIENT_FRAMEWORK_NAME_CONFIG,CommonClientConfigs.CLIENT_FRAMEWORK_VERSION_CONFIGandCommonClientConfigs.CLIENT_FRAMEWORK_ID_CONFIGkeys in the usual way. These configs are not intended to be set by regular applications. Kafka Connect and Kafka Streams both disallow setting these configuration properties and treat them as invalid configurations if set. If other frameworks provides a way for the application to set its own Kafka configs, they should also prevent the application from setting values for the client framework name, version and ID.
The framework name should begin with the reversed Internet domain name for the framework owner, followed by the framework's name. For a framework such as Spring, the framework name would be chosen by Spring and the framework version would reflect the version of Spring.
For Kafka's own frameworks, Kafka Streams and Kafka Connect, Apache Kafka automatically sets the configs as follows:
|
| Kafka Streams | Kafka Connect
| client.framework.name | org.apache.kafka.streams | org.apache.kafka.connect
| client.framework.version | Kafka client version, such as4.5.0 | Kafka client version, such as4.5.0
| client.framework.id | Logical identifier used to group connections for the same Kafka Streams instance (process id) | Connect worker ID
For example, let’s say that Kafka Streams is using the producer in Apache Kafka 4.5.0. It would set the following configurations:
"client.framework.name"="org.apache.kafka.streams"
"client.framework.version"="4.5.0"
"client.framework.id" = "F0DDEDA5-C8C6-493A-B026-F38A13C4E4D8"(the Kafka Streams process id)
Then, inApiVersionsrequest, the following fields would be set:
ClientSoftwareName:"apache-kafka-java"
ClientSoftwareVersion:"4.5.0"
ClientFrameworkName:"org.apache.kafka.streams"
ClientFrameworkVersion:"4.5.0"
ClientFrameworkId:"F0DDEDA5-C8C6-493A-B026-F38A13C4E4D8"
Here's an example of Kafka Connect configurations:
"client.framework.name"="org.apache.kafka.connect"
"client.framework.version"="4.5.0"
"client.framework.id" = "192.168.86.66:8083"
The framework ID in this case is the Connect worker ID.
Metrics
Kafka brokers today do collect metrics for client connections (seeo.a.k.common.network.Selector) and connections are counted by each<clientSoftwareName, clientSoftwareVersion>pair, with a limit of 100 keys.
